llm_response.content:
Below is a complete empirical plan tailored to the data and context you described. I propose a primary IV (shift-share/Bartik) strategy that exploits plausibly exogenous, origin-specific, global institutional portfolio rebalancing to identify the causal effect of institutional ownership on firm governance outcomes. I complement this with a transparent DiD-type robustness that uses instrument-predicted inflow events.

1. Identification Strategy
- Main strategy: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) with a leave-one-country-out shift-share instrument.
- Rationale:
  - Selection/reverse causality is first-order: institutions buy better-governed firms, and firms improve governance to attract institutions. OLS would be upward biased.
  - You have rich ownership microdata by institution origin and sufficient cross-country/time variation (2003–2008) to construct origin-specific aggregate “push” shocks orthogonal to an individual firm’s governance choices.
  - A Bartik-style instrument built from origin-by-style flows in other countries provides strong and plausibly exogenous first-stage variation reflecting fund flows, demographics, and regulation in investors’ home markets rather than target-firm governance changes.
- How the instrument works:
  - Step 1: Define style buckets using pre-period firm characteristics (e.g., global size quintile × book-to-market quintile, 25 cells), fixed at baseline.
  - Step 2: For each investor origin o (e.g., US, UK, Canada, Australia; then aggregated into “common-law origins” if desired) and style s, compute annual changes in that origin’s ownership in firms outside the focal firm’s host country (leave-one-country-out).
  - Step 3: Firm i’s instrument in year t is the baseline exposure of i to style s multiplied by the origin o’s out-of-country style-s flow in t, summed over s (and over o for grouped analyses). Intuition: when US institutions experience exogenous inflows into large-growth globally, firms that looked like large-growth at baseline see more US institutional buying pressure, independent of their own contemporaneous governance.
- Outcomes analyzed:
  - Governance index (GOV41)
  - CEO turnover-performance sensitivity (interaction model)
  - Valuation (Tobin’s Q/market-to-book)

2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable:
  - Continuous: institutional ownership share at firm-year, tailored to the research question component:
    - Total institutional ownership
    - Foreign vs domestic institutional ownership
    - Foreign ownership from common-law origins (e.g., US, UK, Canada, Australia)
    - US vs non-US
    - Independent vs grey institutions
  - Main analysis will focus on foreign common-law institutional ownership share, given the question’s emphasis on origin quality.
- Control group / counterfactual:
  - Within-firm counterfactual using firm fixed effects: the same firm in years with lower instrument-predicted inflows serves as the counterfactual for treated years.
  - The identifying variation is cross-time within firm, induced by exogenous origin-style flows, net of country×year shocks.
- Treatment timing:
  - Continuous exposure each year; we use lagged ownership (t−1) to predict outcomes at t to minimize simultaneity and allow time for governance adjustments.
  - For a DiD robustness, we define an “event” as years when instrument-predicted inflows (into foreign common-law ownership) exceed the firm’s historical 80th percentile; event time is the first such year.
- No RDD in this design.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Relevance: Origin-by-style out-of-country flows are strong predictors of firm-level ownership by that origin. Plausible in 2003–2008 given large cross-border fund flows and style investing.
- Exclusion restriction: Conditional on firm FE, country×year FE, and controls, origin-by-style flows in other countries affect a focal firm’s governance/valuation only via that origin’s ownership in the focal firm, not via other channels.
  - Plausibility: We remove direct host-country contemporaneous shocks with country×year FE; we tie instruments to pre-period styles; we exclude the focal firm’s host country from the flows, weakening reflection and common-shock concerns. Adding style×year FE further soaks up global style performance cycles.
- Monotonicity: Positive origin-specific style flows weakly increase the probability/magnitude of ownership by that origin for all firms more exposed to that style at baseline; no firms systematically decrease ownership when the instrument increases (no “defiers”). Reasonable with passive and style-constrained mandates.
- Stable exposure: Baseline style classification captures a persistent dimension of investor demand; firms do not rapidly jump styles in ways correlated with unobservables. Reasonable over 2003–2008 with size and book-to-market.
- Limited interference/SUTVA: One firm’s instrument does not directly change another’s outcome except via the induced ownership it receives. Leave-one-country-out aggregation and country×year FE reduce within-country general-equilibrium concerns.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigations
- Threat 1: Global style cycles correlate with governance reforms independent of ownership (e.g., large caps globally implement codes; instrument captures that).
  - Mitigations:
    - Include style×year fixed effects (size×BTM×year), so identification comes from differential exposure within a style-year across firms and origins.
    - Control for firm performance and analyst coverage dynamics that correlate with attention/adoption.
    - Placebo: regress pre-period governance (e.g., 2003 GOV41) on future instruments; expect null.
- Threat 2: Reflection within host country or industry (flows co-move with country- or industry-specific reforms).
  - Mitigations:
    - Leave-one-country-out in constructing flows; in robustness, leave-one-country-and-industry-out.
    - Saturate with country×industry×year FE as a robustness (if feasible given sample).
- Threat 3: Measurement error in ownership and governance; dynamic adjustment.
  - Mitigations:
    - Use IV to correct attenuation from ownership measurement error.
    - Use lagged ownership (t−1) and report dynamic distributed lags.
    - For governance persistence, include lagged GOV41; as robustness, use bias-robust estimators (Arellano-Bond/Sys-GMM) for dynamic panels and show similar patterns.

5. R Code Outline
Note: This is executable scaffold code. It assumes CSVs with the necessary fields and a long-form ownership file to construct instruments. Adjust variable names as needed.

Packages
- fixest for FE-IV
- data.table/dplyr for data wrangling
- fastDummies for bucket dummies
- sandwich/multiwayvcov for SEs if needed

R code:

# Packages
library(data.table)
library(dplyr)
library(fixest)
library(fastDummies)

# 1) Load data
# riskmetrics: firm_id, year, gov41
# ownership_long: firm_id, year, origin (e.g., "US","UK","CA","JP",...), own_share (fraction of shares held by institutions from that origin), inst_type ("independent","grey"), investor_domestic (0/1), investor_us (0/1), investor_commonlaw (0/1)
# financials: firm_id, year, country, industry, size_musd, mb, roa, leverage, cash, capex, r_and_d, ppe, foreign_sales, analysts, closely_held, adr, q
# ceo: firm_id, year, ceo_turnover (0/1)
risk <- fread("riskmetrics.csv")
own  <- fread("ownership_long.csv")
fin  <- fread("financials.csv")
ceo  <- fread("ceo.csv")

# 2) Baseline style buckets (size quintile x book-to-market quintile) at baseline year 2003
base_year <- 2003
fin_base <- fin %>% filter(year == base_year) %>%
  mutate(btm = 1/mb) %>%
  group_by() %>%
  mutate(size_q = ntile(size_musd, 5),
         btm_q  = ntile(btm, 5),
         style  = paste0("S", size_q, "_B", btm_q)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(firm_id, style, size_q, btm_q)

# Merge baseline style back to all years (fixed exposure)
fin2 <- fin %>% left_join(fin_base, by = "firm_id")

# 3) Define origin groups of interest
# Mark common-law origins: e.g., US, UK, CA, AU, NZ, IE, SG, HK (adjust list as appropriate)
commonlaw_origins <- c("US","UK","CA","AU","NZ","IE","SG","HK")
own <- own %>%
  mutate(origin_group = case_when(origin %in% commonlaw_origins ~ "commonlaw",
                                  TRUE ~ "other"))

# Compute foreign flag: investor is foreign if origin != firm's country
own <- own %>% left_join(fin2 %>% select(firm_id, year, country), by = c("firm_id","year")) %>%
  mutate(foreign_flag = as.integer(origin != country))

# 4) Construct treatment variables (ownership shares by group)
# Example: foreign common-law institutional ownership share per firm-year
own_fc <- own %>%
  filter(foreign_flag == 1, origin_group == "commonlaw") %>%
  group_by(firm_id, year) %>%
  summarise(own_fc = sum(own_share, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# 5) Construct leave-one-country-out origin-by-style flows (instrument)
# First, attach baseline style to ownership data
own_s <- own %>%
  left_join(fin2 %>% select(firm_id, style), by = "firm_id")

# Aggregate ownership by origin, style, country, year
agg_oscy <- own_s %>%
  group_by(origin, style, country, year) %>%
  summarise(own_share_sum = sum(own_share, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# For each origin, style, and year, compute total outside each country (leave-one-country-out)
# We'll create a table with origin, style, year, country_excluded, out_of_country_own
total_osy <- agg_oscy %>%
  group_by(origin, style, year) %>%
  summarise(total_own = sum(own_share_sum, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

loc_oscy <- agg_oscy %>%
  left_join(total_osy, by = c("origin","style","year")) %>%
  mutate(out_of_ctry_own = pmax(total_own - own_share_sum, 0)) %>%
  select(origin, style, country_excl = country, year, out_of_ctry_own)

# Compute year-over-year change in out-of-country ownership by origin-style, for each excluded country
loc_oscy <- loc_oscy %>%
  arrange(origin, style, country_excl, year) %>%
  group_by(origin, style, country_excl) %>%
  mutate(d_out_of_ctry_own = out_of_ctry_own - dplyr::lag(out_of_ctry_own)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Collapse to common-law origins for the instrument (sum flows across those origins)
loc_oscy_cl <- loc_oscy %>%
  mutate(origin_group = ifelse(origin %in% commonlaw_origins, "commonlaw", "other")) %>%
  group_by(origin_group, style, country_excl, year) %>%
  summarise(d_flow = sum(d_out_of_ctry_own, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(origin_group == "commonlaw") %>%
  select(style, country_excl, year, d_flow_cl = d_flow)

# 6) Build firm-level instrument: baseline style exposure x origin-group flow (by excluded country = firm country)
# Compute style dummies for baseline exposure
style_mat <- fin_base %>%
  select(firm_id, style) %>%
  fastDummies::dummy_cols("style", remove_selected_columns = TRUE)

# Merge to panel and flows
panel <- fin2 %>%
  select(firm_id, year, country, industry, size_musd, mb, roa, leverage, cash, capex, r_and_d, ppe, foreign_sales, analysts, closely_held, adr, q) %>%
  left_join(risk, by = c("firm_id","year")) %>%
  left_join(own_fc, by = c("firm_id","year")) %>%
  left_join(style_mat, by = "firm_id") %>%
  group_by(firm_id) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(own_fc_lag = dplyr::lag(own_fc),
         roa_lag = dplyr::lag(roa),
         q_lag = dplyr::lag(q),
         gov41_lag = dplyr::lag(gov41)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Create instrument as sum over styles: exposure * d_flow_cl for the firm's country and year
# First, reshape flows wide by style for easy multiplication
flows_wide <- loc_oscy_cl %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = style, values_from = d_flow_cl, values_fill = 0)

# Merge flows by firm country and year
panel <- panel %>%
  left_join(flows_wide, by = c("country" = "country_excl", "year"))

# Compute Z = sum_s exposure_i,s * d_flow_cl_{s, -country, t}
style_cols <- grep("^style_", names(panel), value = TRUE)  # baseline style dummies
flow_cols  <- gsub("style_", "", style_cols)               # style names used in flows_wide

# Align exposure dummies to flow columns
for (j in seq_along(style_cols)) {
  sc <- style_cols[j]
  fc <- sub("^style_", "", sc)
  if (!(fc %in% names(panel))) panel[[fc]] <- 0
  # multiply exposure dummy by flow
  panel[[paste0("Z_part_", fc)]] <- panel[[sc]] * panel[[fc]]
}

# Sum parts to form instrument
z_cols <- grep("^Z_part_", names(panel), value = TRUE)
panel <- panel %>%
  mutate(Z_fc = rowSums(across(all_of(z_cols)), na.rm = TRUE))

# Clean NAs
panel <- panel %>%
  mutate(own_fc_lag = ifelse(is.na(own_fc_lag), 0, own_fc_lag),
         Z_fc = ifelse(is.na(Z_fc), 0, Z_fc))

# 7) Fixed effects identifiers
panel <- panel %>%
  mutate(firm_fe = firm_id,
         ctry_year = interaction(country, year, drop = TRUE),
         ind_year  = interaction(industry, year, drop = TRUE))

# 8) Main specification: Governance outcome (t) on lagged foreign common-law ownership (t-1), IVed by Z_fc (t)
# Include controls at t-1 and FE
# Note: style×year FE robustness shown later
main_gov_iv <- feols(gov41 ~ gov41_lag + leverage + cash + size_musd + mb + analysts + closely_held + adr | firm_fe + ctry_year,
                     iv = ~ own_fc_lag ~ Z_fc,
                     data = panel,
                     cluster = ~ firm_id + year)

summary(main_gov_iv)

# 9) Valuation outcome: Q (t) on lagged foreign common-law ownership (t-1), IV
val_iv <- feols(q ~ q_lag + leverage + cash + size_musd + mb + analysts + closely_held + adr | firm_fe + ctry_year,
                iv = ~ own_fc_lag ~ Z_fc,
                data = panel,
                cluster = ~ firm_id + year)

summary(val_iv)

# 10) CEO turnover-performance sensitivity (LPM with FE-IV; instrument IO and its interaction)
# Define performance: stock or accounting; use roa_lag (higher = better)
# Expect baseline beta_perf < 0; interaction beta_io_perf < 0 if IO strengthens discipline
panel2 <- panel %>% left_join(ceo, by = c("firm_id","year")) %>%
  mutate(io_x_perf = own_fc_lag * roa_lag,
         Z_x_perf  = Z_fc * roa_lag)

turn_iv <- feols(ceo_turnover ~ roa_lag + leverage + size_musd + mb | firm_fe + ctry_year,
                 iv = ~ own_fc_lag + io_x_perf ~ Z_fc + Z_x_perf,
                 data = panel2,
                 cluster = ~ firm_id + year)

summary(turn_iv)

# 11) Robustness A: Add style×year FE to soak up global style cycles
# Build style-year FE using baseline style
panel$style_year <- interaction(panel$style, panel$year, drop = TRUE)

gov_iv_stylefe <- feols(gov41 ~ gov41_lag + leverage + cash + size_musd + mb + analysts + closely_held + adr | firm_fe + ctry_year + style_year,
                        iv = ~ own_fc_lag ~ Z_fc,
                        data = panel,
                        cluster = ~ firm_id + year)
summary(gov_iv_stylefe)

# 12) Robustness B: Pre-trend/placebo – regress baseline governance (2003) on future instrument average (2004–2006)
future_Z <- panel %>%
  filter(year >= 2004, year <= 2006) %>%
  group_by(firm_id) %>%
  summarise(futZ = mean(Z_fc, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

placebo <- fin2 %>%
  filter(year == 2003) %>%
  left_join(risk %>% filter(year == 2003), by = c("firm_id","year")) %>%
  left_join(future_Z, by = "firm_id")

placebo_mod <- feols(gov41 ~ futZ + size_musd + mb | country, data = placebo, cluster = ~ country)
summary(placebo_mod)

6. Expected Results
- Sign of main effects:
  - Governance (GOV41): Positive. Greater foreign institutional ownership from common-law origins should increase adoption of pro-shareholder practices.
  - CEO turnover-performance sensitivity: Stronger. The interaction of IO with performance should make turnover more sensitive to poor performance (more negative slope on performance).
  - Valuation (Q): Positive. Better governance and monitoring increase expected cash flows and reduce private benefits extraction, lifting Q.
- Magnitudes (priors, per 10 percentage point increase in foreign common-law IO):
  - GOV41: +0.10 to +0.20 standard deviations.
  - Turnover-performance sensitivity: for a one-SD improvement in performance, the probability of turnover falls by an additional 0.5–1.0 percentage points (i.e., stronger negative slope).
  - Q: +3% to +5%.
- Heterogeneity:
  - Effects larger in civil-law host countries and among firms with weaker baseline governance, more closely held shares, or limited analyst coverage.
  - Independent institutions drive stronger effects than grey institutions.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)
- C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10 with leave-one-country-out origin×style flows) — 1
- C2: Exclusion restriction (flows affect outcomes only through ownership given FE and controls) — 0
  - Concern: residual global style governance waves; addressed with style×year FE and placebos but not provable.
- C3: Monotonicity (no defiers to flow shocks) — 1
- C4: Stable exposure (baseline style classification is persistent and predetermined) — 1
- C5: Limited interference/common shocks controlled (leave-one-country-out, country×year FE, robustness with industry×year) — 1

Notes and Extensions
- Estimate analogous models for domestic institutions, non-US institutions, civil-law origins, and grey vs independent to map mechanisms.
- Use dynamic distributed lags of ownership to study timing of governance changes.
- Implement a stacked DiD as robustness: define events by high instrument-predicted inflows, match on propensity, and estimate event-time coefficients for GOV41; check for pre-trends.
